title: Building AI Products That Actually Work — Ben Hylak (Raindrop), Sid Bendre (Oleve)

domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: Ben is building Sentry for AI products and the core thesis is that AI apps lack concrete exceptions, requiring production signals to detect issues. Raindrop is a developer observability platform while Oleve builds consumer productivity apps, spanning both builder and end-user verticals. The talk focuses on monitoring deployed AI products via signals and scaling consumer products through the Trellis framework. Assumes working knowledge of evals, LLM-as-judge, structured output, and production AI systems. Recorded two-speaker conference presentation at AI Engineer World's Fair. All evidence anchors are graded as said_in_transcript from the transcript source.

summary: Ben Hylak (Raindrop) and Sid Bendre (Oleve) discuss building AI products that work, emphasizing iteration over evals alone. Ben shares failure anecdotes from Virgin Money, Google Cloud, and Grok to show even major providers ship broken products. He argues that while structured output is improving, communication difficulty and increasing undefined behavior mean development won't get much easier, disputing Paul Graham's claim that AGI ends prompt engineering. He critiques three eval misconceptions: that they measure overall quality (Goodhart's law), that LLM-as-judge works reliably for subjective tasks (best companies use autogradable evals and curated datasets), and that offline evals can simply move to production data. Because AI apps throw no concrete exceptions, Ben introduces signals as ground truthy indicators of performance. Explicit signals include thumbs up/down, copy rate (as ChatGPT tracks), preference data, regenerations, and syntax errors. Implicit signals involve detecting refusals, task failure, and user frustration through clustering. The anatomy of an AI issue combines signals with user intents, and teams must constantly explore and refine these patterns—like Sentry tags—through data review and user conversations. Sid then presents Trellis, Oleve's framework for scaling viral consumer AI products at ~$6M ARR with a tiny team. Trellis rests on three axioms—discretization (bucket the infinite output space), prioritization (rank by business impact), and recursive refinement. Its six steps: launch an MVP agent to collect user data, classify usage into intents, convert intents into semi-deterministic workflows that are self-attributable and self-bound, prioritize workflows (naive: volume; better: volume × negative sentiment; best: negative sentiment × volume × estimated achievable delta × strategic relevance), analyze failure patterns within workflows, and recurse deeper. The goal is engineered, repeatable, testable magic—not accidental—allowing small teams to scale reliably without eliminating AI's nondeterministic appeal.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

takeaways: Iteration and real-world signals matter more than evals alone for building reliable AI products.
AI apps throw no concrete exceptions, so teams need signals—ground truthy indicators of performance—to find issues.
Explicit signals include thumbs up/down, copy rate, preference data, regenerations, and errors; implicit signals include detected refusals, task failure, and user frustration.
The anatomy of an AI issue combines signals with user intents; teams must constantly explore, define, and refine these patterns.
Evals don't measure overall product quality, LLM-as-judge is unreliable for subjective tasks, and moving offline evals online is expensive and limited.
Trellis—Oleve's framework—uses discretization, prioritization, and recursive refinement to scale viral AI products systematically.
Workflows should be self-attributable, deterministic, and self-bound so teams can improve them without spillover into other workflows.
Prioritization should incorporate negative sentiment, volume, estimated achievable delta, and strategic relevance—not just volume.
The goal is engineered, repeatable, testable, attributable AI magic—not accidental outcomes.
Even major providers like OpenAI, Google, and xAI ship broken AI products, underscoring the need for continuous monitoring.

sections.title: Introduction and Speaker Backgrounds
sections.summary: Ben Hylak introduces himself (CTO of Raindrop, ex-Apple, ex-SpaceX) and Sid Bendre (co-founder of Oleve), framing the talk around iteration for AI products.

sections.title: AI Product Failures and the Current State
sections.summary: Ben shares anecdotes of AI failures from Virgin Money, Google Cloud, and Grok to show even major providers ship broken products, while noting the potential of focused use cases and small models.

sections.title: Will AI Products Get Easier to Build?
sections.summary: Ben argues that while structured output improved, communication difficulty and more undefined behavior mean building AI products remains hard, disputing Paul Graham's view on AGI and prompt engineering.

sections.title: Misconceptions About Evals
sections.summary: Ben critiques three eval myths: that they measure product quality, that LLM judges work, and that offline evals can move online. He concludes reliable AI apps need real signals.

sections.title: Signals and AI Issue Anatomy
sections.summary: Ben defines signals as ground truthy indicators of app performance, distinguishing explicit signals (thumbs up/down, copy rate, preference data, regenerations, errors) from implicit signals (detected refusals, task failure, user frustration). The anatomy of an AI issue combines signals with user intents. Teams must constantly explore, define, and refine issue patterns through data review and user conversations.

sections.title: Sid's Trellis Framework for Scaling Viral AI Products
sections.summary: Sid presents Trellis, Oleve's framework for systematically scaling viral consumer AI products. Three axioms—discretization, prioritization, recursive refinement—drive six steps: launch MVP agent, classify intents, convert to semi-deterministic workflows, prioritize by impact, analyze failure patterns, and recurse. Prioritization should weigh negative sentiment, volume, estimated achievable delta, and strategic relevance. Workflows should be self-attributable and self-bound for reliable team velocity.

limitations: Evals only catch issues you already know about
LM judges are largely unreliable for subjective tasks
Evaling production data is expensive, hard to set up, and misses emerging patterns
AI apps produce no concrete exceptions, making traditional error monitoring insufficient
Volume-only prioritization leaves room for improving overall satisfaction
quantitativeClaims: Oleve grew viral apps to over 6 million ARR with four people
Ben worked at Apple for almost four years
Oleve scaled viral products to around $6 million profitably
Oleve generated about half a billion views on socials
One Oleve product reached #4 on App Store Education charts in 2024 and #5 in 2025
